10X-Legal Prototype — Data Collected and Activities Completed

Reporting Period: January 19 – April 9, 2026 (~12 weeks)
Section: Level 1 — Quantifying the Work

Project Overview

10X-Legal is a full-stack case-tracking dashboard prototype for legal professionals. The team designed, built, tested, and deployed a production web application — React/TypeScript frontend, Express/PostgreSQL backend, AWS cloud infrastructure provisioned through Pulumi — and populated it with publicly available Utah court records.

This section quantifies both halves of the work: Part A reports the dataset the team collected and cleaned, and Part B reports the engineering activities completed. Together they form the foundation for the insights and impact discussion that follows in later sections.

Part A — Data Collected

The team ingested publicly released Utah court records covering felony sexual-exploitation, intimate-image, and sexual-extortion cases. After cleaning, normalization, and de-duplication the database contains:

A.2 Filing Activity Over Time

Filing volume rose steadily from 2021 to a peak of 220 cases in 2023, then plateaued. The 2025 figure (148) reflects only filings recorded through the most recent data dump and is therefore partial.

Figure A1 — Cases by filing year, 2021 through 2025.

A.3 Geographic Distribution

Cases are concentrated in the populous Wasatch Front districts. The Third District (Salt Lake County) alone accounts for 30.2% of all cases ingested; together Districts 2, 3, and 4 hold 73.6% of the dataset.

Figure A2 — Cases broken out across Utah’s eight judicial districts.

Within those districts, ten courts handle 88% of the volume. Salt Lake City alone has more than double the caseload of any other court.

Figure A3 — Top 10 courts by case volume.

A.4 Charge Distribution

The dataset is dominated by a single charge category: Sexual Exploitation of a Minor, which accounts for 650 cases (71.1%). The next four largest charge categories together account for an additional 26.2%, leaving twelve other charge types making up the remaining 2.6%.

Figure A4 — Distribution of charges across the 914 cases.

A.5 Case Outcomes

Of the 914 cases ingested, 901 (98.6%) reached a recorded disposition. Two outcome codes dominate the dataset:

Figure A5 — Case disposition outcomes recorded in the source data.

A.6 Attorney Roster

The 914 cases produced 449 unique attorney records. Defense attorneys outnumber prosecuting attorneys roughly 2-to-1, reflecting the use of private defense counsel and public defenders alongside a smaller, more concentrated pool of prosecuting attorneys.

Figure A6 — 449 attorneys split by side.

Caseload concentration tells a striking story. A single prosecutor — Jeffrey Gray — appears on 116 cases, more than the next two prosecutors combined and over 12% of the entire dataset.

Figure A7 — Top 10 prosecuting attorneys by caseload.

On the defense side the distribution is also concentrated, with William C Morison-Knox leading at 70 cases and the catch-all "State Public Defender" entry covering an additional 49.

Figure A8 — Top 10 defense attorneys by caseload.

A.7 Data Pipeline Activities

Reaching a clean, queryable dataset required multiple iterations on the spreadsheet-to-database mapping:

  • Attorney name normalization — converted records from "Last, First" all-caps format to title-cased "First Last" so the same attorney was no longer split across multiple records.
  • Composite case identity — replaced the single-column case-number unique constraint with a composite (case_number, district_number) index so identical case numbers from different districts no longer collided into a single row.
  • Re-import deduplication — added upsert logic so subsequent data dumps update existing rows instead of inserting duplicates.
  • Many-to-many attorney relationships — introduced a case_attorneys junction table and migrated all four legacy attorney columns into it, enabling cases to track multiple prosecutors and defenders accurately.
  • Audit trail — every import is recorded in the import_history table with row counts, success/failure status, and an error log; every administrator action is logged in audit_log.

B.3 Application Features Delivered

B.3.1 Backend REST API (Express 5 + PostgreSQL)

Ten route modules totaling approximately 2,150 lines of HTTP handler code:

Route ModuleResponsibility
auth.routes.tsRegistration, login, JWT issuance, refresh tokens
users.routes.tsUser profile CRUD
cases.routes.tsCase CRUD, search, filtering
attorneys.routes.tsAttorney records and case associations
judges.routes.tsJudge records and assignments
firms.routes.tsLaw firm registry
deadlines.routes.tsCase deadline tracking
documents.routes.tsFile upload/download (multer)
admin.routes.tsUser management, data import, audit log, system stats

Database (PostgreSQL on AWS RDS): 11 relational tables — users, refresh_tokens, law_firms, attorneys, judges, cases, case_attorneys (junction), documents, deadlines, import_history, audit_log — supported by 10 performance indexes and inline migration logic.

Authentication model: four user roles (client, lawyer, legal-official, admin) with bcrypt password hashing, JWT access tokens, and refresh-token rotation.
